## Theoretical distributions

**Theoretical distributions** describe idealised properties — not the frequencies in one dataset, but the likelihood of values in an abstract "population." They're fully described by a handful of *parameters*.

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:20px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), *Data Analysis for Business, Economics, and Policy*, Ch. 3
:::

## The normal distribution

::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
- Bell-shaped, symmetric — mean, median, and mode coincide
- Fully described by two parameters: $\mu$ (the mean) and $\sigma$ (the standard deviation)
- Examples: height, IQ, measurement error
:::
::: {.col}
```{ojs}
{
  const rng = d3.randomNormal(0, 1)
  const sample = Array.from({ length: 4000 }, rng)
  return Plot.plot({
    ariaLabel: "Histogram of a simulated normal distribution",
    ariaDescription: "4,000 simulated draws from a standard normal distribution, shown as a histogram. The shape is symmetric and bell-shaped, peaking at zero and falling away evenly on both sides.",
    height: 240,
    x: { label: "x", domain: [-4, 4] },
    y: { label: "% of draws", percent: true },
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(sample, Plot.binX({ y: "proportion" },
        { x: d => d, thresholds: 30, fill: "#457b9d", fillOpacity: 0.8 })),
      Plot.ruleX([0]),
    ]
  })
}
```
:::
:::

## The log-normal distribution

::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
- Normal arises from **summing** many small, independent effects. Log-normal arises from **multiplying** them — and since $\log(a \times b) = \log a + \log b$, the log of such a variable is itself a sum, so it's approximately normal
- Transform a normal $x$ with $e^x$ and you get exactly this: always non-negative, long right tail
- Examples: income, firm size, our reaction-time data — each the result of many small multiplicative factors (attention, motor noise, distraction, ...)
:::
::: {.col}
```{ojs}
{
  const rng = d3.randomLogNormal(0, 0.5)
  const sample = Array.from({ length: 4000 }, rng)
  const cutoff = d3.quantile(sample.slice().sort(d3.ascending), 0.99)
  return Plot.plot({
    ariaLabel: "Histogram of a simulated log-normal distribution",
    ariaDescription: "4,000 simulated draws from a log-normal distribution, shown as a histogram. The shape is right-skewed: most values cluster near zero with a long tail of larger values, unlike the symmetric normal distribution.",
    height: 240,
    x: { label: "x", domain: [0, cutoff] },
    y: { label: "% of draws", percent: true },
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(sample.filter(d => d <= cutoff), Plot.binX({ y: "proportion" },
        { x: d => d, thresholds: 30, fill: "#2d6a4f", fillOpacity: 0.8 })),
      Plot.ruleX([0]),
    ]
  })
}
```
:::
:::

## The power-law distribution

::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
- Also called the **Pareto** distribution — large extreme values are common at any scale
- Examples: city population, word frequency, wealth
:::
::: {.col}
```{ojs}
{
  const alpha = 2.5, xmin = 1
  const sample = Array.from({ length: 4000 }, () => xmin * Math.pow(1 - Math.random(), -1 / alpha))
  const cutoff = d3.quantile(sample.slice().sort(d3.ascending), 0.97)
  return Plot.plot({
    ariaLabel: "Histogram of a simulated power-law (Pareto) distribution",
    ariaDescription: "4,000 simulated draws from a power-law distribution, shown as a histogram. Almost all values are small and close to the minimum, with a very long thin tail of much larger values — extreme values are far more common here than in a normal or log-normal distribution.",
    height: 240,
    x: { label: "x", domain: [0, cutoff] },
    y: { label: "% of draws", percent: true },
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(sample.filter(d => d <= cutoff), Plot.binX({ y: "proportion" },
        { x: d => d, thresholds: 30, fill: "#e63946", fillOpacity: 0.8 })),
      Plot.ruleX([0]),
    ]
  })
}
```
:::
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:8px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 3 — shapes simulated here to show each family's characteristic silhouette
:::

## The uniform distribution

::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
- Flat — every value in a range is equally likely
- Fully described by two parameters: the minimum and maximum
- Mean and median sit at the midpoint, but there's no peak — no value is any more "typical" than another
- Examples: random number generators, rounding error, waiting time within a fixed interval
:::
::: {.col}
```{ojs}
{
  const rng = d3.randomUniform(0, 10)
  const sample = Array.from({ length: 4000 }, rng)
  return Plot.plot({
    ariaLabel: "Histogram of a simulated uniform distribution",
    ariaDescription: "4,000 simulated draws from a uniform distribution between 0 and 10, shown as a histogram. The bars are roughly the same height across the whole range — every value is equally likely, with no peak.",
    height: 240,
    x: { label: "x", domain: [0, 10] },
    y: { label: "% of draws", percent: true },
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(sample, Plot.binX({ y: "proportion" },
        { x: d => d, thresholds: 20, fill: "#f4a261", fillOpacity: 0.8 })),
      Plot.ruleX([0]),
    ]
  })
}
```
:::
:::

## The Bernoulli distribution

::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
- The simplest distribution — a single trial with two possible outcomes
- Fully described by one parameter: $p$, the probability of success
- The building block every other distribution on this page is made from
- Examples: a single coin flip, one pass/fail test, one yes/no question
:::
::: {.col}
```{ojs}
{
  const p = 0.3
  const sample = Array.from({ length: 4000 }, d3.randomBernoulli(p))
  return Plot.plot({
    ariaLabel: "Bar chart of a simulated Bernoulli distribution",
    ariaDescription: "4,000 simulated draws from a Bernoulli distribution with a 30% probability of success, shown as two bars. The bar at zero (failure) is taller, at roughly 70% of draws, and the bar at one (success) is shorter, at roughly 30%.",
    height: 240,
    x: { label: "Outcome", domain: [-0.5, 1.5], ticks: [0, 1] },
    y: { label: "% of draws", percent: true },
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(sample, Plot.groupX({ y: "proportion" },
        { x: d => d, interval: 1, fill: "#1d3557", fillOpacity: 0.8 })),
      Plot.ruleX([0]),
    ]
  })
}
```
:::
:::

## The binomial distribution

::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
- The number of successes across $n$ independent Bernoulli trials
- Described by two parameters: $n$ (number of trials) and $p$ (probability of success on each)
- As $n$ grows, its shape approaches the normal distribution — a preview of why the normal shows up so often
- Examples: defective items in a batch, correct answers on a multiple-choice test
:::
::: {.col}
```{ojs}
{
  const n = 20, p = 0.3
  const sample = Array.from({ length: 4000 }, d3.randomBinomial(n, p))
  return Plot.plot({
    ariaLabel: "Histogram of a simulated binomial distribution",
    ariaDescription: "4,000 simulated draws of the number of successes in 20 trials with a 30% success probability, shown as a histogram. The shape is roughly symmetric and bell-shaped, peaking around 6 successes — an early preview of how the binomial approaches the normal shape as the number of trials grows.",
    height: 240,
    x: { label: "Number of successes (out of 20)", domain: [-0.5, n + 0.5] },
    y: { label: "% of draws", percent: true },
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(sample, Plot.groupX({ y: "proportion" },
        { x: d => d, interval: 1, fill: "#e9c46a", fillOpacity: 0.8 })),
      Plot.ruleX([0]),
    ]
  })
}
```
:::
:::

## The Poisson distribution

::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
- The number of events in a fixed interval, given a constant average rate
- Described by a single parameter: $\lambda$ (lambda), the average rate itself
- Mean and variance are both exactly $\lambda$ — a distinctive fingerprint of this distribution
- Examples: customer arrivals per hour, emails per day, typos per page
:::
::: {.col}
```{ojs}
{
  const lambda = 4
  const sample = Array.from({ length: 4000 }, d3.randomPoisson(lambda))
  return Plot.plot({
    ariaLabel: "Histogram of a simulated Poisson distribution",
    ariaDescription: "4,000 simulated draws from a Poisson distribution with an average rate of 4 events, shown as a histogram. The shape is right-skewed and concentrated on small whole numbers, peaking around 3 to 4 events.",
    height: 240,
    x: { label: "Number of events", domain: [-0.5, 15.5] },
    y: { label: "% of draws", percent: true },
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(sample, Plot.groupX({ y: "proportion" },
        { x: d => d, interval: 1, fill: "#e63946", fillOpacity: 0.8 })),
      Plot.ruleX([0]),
    ]
  })
}
```
:::
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:8px;"}
Not covered in this chapter of the textbook, but useful to have in view.
:::

## Our data, and its log

If reaction times are log-normal, the **log** of reaction time should look roughly normal.

Let's work through this together in Excel — a histogram of the raw reaction times, then a histogram of their log. Compare the shapes before we look at the answer.

::: {.fragment}
```{ojs}
{
  const rtSorted = rt.slice().sort(d3.ascending)
  const rtCut    = d3.quantile(rtSorted, 0.98)
  const logRt    = rt.map(Math.log)

  const p1 = Plot.plot({
    ariaLabel: "Histogram of the class's raw reaction times",
    ariaDescription: "A histogram of the class's actual reaction times in milliseconds, trimmed to the bottom 98% to exclude the most extreme outlier. The shape is right-skewed, matching the log-normal prediction.",
    height: 240, width: 380,
    x: { label: "Reaction time (ms)", domain: [0, rtCut] },
    y: { label: "% of trials", percent: true },
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(rt.filter(d => d <= rtCut), Plot.binX({ y: "proportion" },
        { x: d => d, thresholds: 20, fill: "#457b9d", fillOpacity: 0.8 })),
      Plot.ruleX([0]),
    ]
  })
  const p2 = Plot.plot({
    ariaLabel: "Histogram of the log of the class's reaction times",
    ariaDescription: "A histogram of the natural log of the same reaction times. The shape is much closer to symmetric and bell-shaped than the raw histogram beside it, supporting the claim that reaction time is log-normally distributed.",
    height: 240, width: 380,
    x: { label: "log(reaction time)" },
    y: { label: "% of trials", percent: true },
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(logRt, Plot.binX({ y: "proportion" },
        { x: d => d, thresholds: 20, fill: "#2d6a4f", fillOpacity: 0.8 })),
      Plot.ruleX([0]),
    ]
  })

  return html`<div style="display:flex;gap:24px;justify-content:center;">${p1}${p2}</div>`
}
```

Raw reaction times (blue) are right-skewed with a long tail. Their log (green) looks far closer to symmetric and bell-shaped — exactly what the log-normal claim predicts.
:::
